content: Botulism is a severe paralytic condition caused by a neurotoxin produced by Clostridium botulinum. While supportive care, including intensive care, is essential, the effectiveness of other medical treatments remains uncertain. This review aimed to evaluate the impact of medical treatments on outcomes such as mortality, length of hospitalization, duration of mechanical ventilation, duration of tube or parenteral feeding, and the risk of adverse events in cases of botulism. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that investigated medical treatments for the four main types of botulism: infant intestinal botulism, foodborne botulism, wound botulism, and adult intestinal toxemia. Potential treatments assessed included equine serum trivalent botulism antitoxin, human-derived botulinum immune globulin intravenous (BIG-IV), plasma exchange, 3,4-diaminopyridine, and guanidine. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and clinical trial registries was conducted, with the most recent search completed in early 2019. Only one RCT met the inclusion criteria. This trial evaluated the use of BIG-IV in treating infant botulism and included 59 participants in the treatment group and 63 participants in the control group. The control group received an immune globulin that had no effect on botulinum toxin. Participants were monitored throughout their hospitalization to assess the outcomes of interest. The trial showed no deaths in either the treatment or control groups, making it impossible to estimate the effect of BIG-IV on mortality. However, the study demonstrated that BIG-IV reduced the average duration of hospitalization. The treatment group had a mean hospital stay of 2.60 weeks (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.95 to 3.25), compared to 5.70 weeks (95% CI: 4.40 to 7.00) in the control group, with a mean difference (MD) of -3.10 weeks (95% CI: -4.52 to -1.68). This evidence was of moderate certainty. BIG-IV also appeared to reduce the duration of mechanical ventilation. The treatment group required ventilation for an average of 1.80 weeks (95% CI: 1.20 to 2.40), compared to 4.40 weeks (95% CI: 3.00 to 5.80) in the control group, with an MD of -2.60 weeks (95% CI: -4.06 to -1.14). However, this evidence was of low certainty. Similarly, BIG-IV reduced the duration of tube or parenteral feeding. The treatment group required feeding support for an average of 3.60 weeks (95% CI: 1.70 to 5.50), compared to 10.00 weeks (95% CI: 6.85 to 13.15) in the control group, with an MD of -6.40 weeks (95% CI: -10.00 to -2.80). This evidence was of moderate certainty. There was no significant difference between the treatment and control groups in the proportion of participants experiencing adverse events or complications. In the BIG-IV group, 63.08% of participants experienced adverse events, compared to 68.75% in the control group. The risk ratio was 0.92 (95% CI: 0.72 to 1.18), with an absolute risk reduction of 0.06 (95% CI: -0.11 to 0.22). This evidence was of moderate certainty. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that BIG-IV is likely to reduce the duration of hospitalization and tube or parenteral feeding in cases of infant botulism and may reduce the duration of mechanical ventilation. Adverse events were not more frequent with BIG-IV compared to placebo. However, no evidence was found to support the use of other medical treatments, such as equine serum trivalent botulism antitoxin, for botulism.
